911.title: Craft the job
911.hook: researchers found hospital cleaners who shaped their jobs around patients' care found more meaning (Wrzesniewski and Dutton, 2001)
911.howItsDone: People who practice job crafting look for small changes within their role: adjusting a task, building a relationship, or reframing the work around the people it serves; some also hold their daily tasks as an offering, in the spirit of Herbert's poem.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was one thing: every switch has a toll, and Ecclesiastes says do it with thy might. Your line was practicing the way back. Today, the same job, done two different ways.

Two people clean the same hospital ward. Same mop, same pay, same list. One of them describes the job as cleaning rooms. The other talks about the patients: which one likes the blinds open, which one hasn't had a visitor, how to time the floors so nobody is woken. When researchers Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton looked at people like these, the second kind of cleaner saw the work as part of healing, and found more meaning in it. Nobody had rewritten their job description. They had reshaped the job themselves. Today: job crafting.
screen: `SAME MOP, SAME LIST.` → `THE BLINDS, THE VISITOR, THE FLOORS.` → `THEY CHANGED IT THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Wrzesniewski and Dutton called this job crafting: the ways people quietly reshape the work they've been given. Their paper describes three. First, the tasks. You can add, drop or change what you do, or how you do it. The cleaner who times the floors so a patient can sleep has changed a task, without asking anyone. Second, the relationships: who you deal with, and how. Some cleaners talked with patients and families, and saw themselves as part of the care team. The list never mentioned conversation; they added it. Third, the way you see it. Cleaning rooms, or helping people heal: the work is identical, and the meaning isn't. Now a neighbor from much further back. The poet and priest George Herbert wrote a short poem called The Elixir, about doing ordinary things for God. One stanza says: "Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, Makes that and th' action fine." For Herbert, the sweeping stays sweeping. What changes is what it's done for, and that changes both the room and the act. The researchers don't speak of God, and Herbert didn't run a study. They describe something that rhymes: the same task can be lifted by how it's held. Fourth, a caution. Job crafting isn't a way to excuse bad pay or bad bosses; some jobs need changing from the outside, too. But inside a lot of work there's a little room to move, and that room is yours.
screen: `CHANGE THE TASKS.` · `CHANGE THE RELATIONSHIPS.` · `CHANGE HOW YOU SEE IT.` · `WHO SWEEPS A ROOM.` · then, large: `CRAFT THE JOB.`

segments.voice: Hold your own work in mind, paid or unpaid, a job, a home, a study, a care you give, and breathe slowly. Picture one task you do often, one person your work touches, and what the work is for underneath the list. Don't decide anything yet; just let one possibility rise, and hold it.
Job crafting. The ways people quietly reshape the tasks, relationships and meaning of the work they've been given. Today's word.
Your line: that room is yours. Same mop, same list, and still a different job. Until tomorrow.

912.title: Unpaid, not unvalued
912.hook: caring, housework and volunteering are work, and traditions honor them
912.carry: I saw what you did, and it mattered
912.howItsDone: Sikhs perform seva at gurdwaras by cooking and serving langar, cleaning and caring for visitors; in some Jewish homes the poem from Proverbs 31 is sung at the Friday night table.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was job crafting: hospital cleaners who reshaped their own jobs, and Herbert's line about sweeping a room. Your line was that room is yours. Today, the work nobody pays for at all.

Who washed the dishes after dinner last night? Who sat up with the feverish child, drove the grandparent to the appointment, folded the laundry, coached the team, made the casserole for the neighbor after the funeral? None of it shows up on a paycheck. When someone asks, so what do you do, almost none of it gets mentioned. And yet a household, a street, a congregation would start to fall apart without it. Today: unpaid.
screen: `DISHES, FEVERS, RIDES, CASSEROLES.` → `NOT ON ANY PAYCHECK.` → `WITHOUT IT, THINGS FALL APART.`

segments.voice: First, a name for it. Unpaid work is still work. Caring for children or the sick, keeping a home running, volunteering: they take time, skill and energy, just like paid jobs. Only the money is missing, and money is not the only measure of worth. Second, a very old portrait. The last chapter of the book of Proverbs, in the Hebrew Bible, praises a capable woman. Much of what it honors is the work of a household: she rises while it's still night, provides food, makes cloth, opens her hand to the poor. One verse says, "She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness." In some Jewish homes, this poem is sung at the Friday night table. Housework, in that text, isn't invisible. It's sung about. Third, a word from Sikh tradition: seva, selfless service. At a gurdwara, the Sikh place of worship, volunteers cook and serve langar, a free communal meal open to anyone who walks in. Others wash the dishes, sweep the floors, or care for visitors' shoes. Nobody is paid. In Sikh teaching, this is not a lesser task than worship; seva is itself a way of serving God and the community, and anyone may take part, whatever their standing. Fourth, what this asks of us. If unpaid work is real work, then the people doing it deserve real thanks. Not a vague nod at holidays, but a specific word: I saw what you did, and it mattered.
screen: `UNPAID WORK IS STILL WORK.` · `THE BREAD OF IDLENESS.` · `SEVA, SELFLESS SERVICE.` · `I SAW WHAT YOU DID.` · then, large: `UNPAID, NOT UNVALUED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a meal someone cooked for you, a bed someone made, a hard day someone sat through with you, and let one person stand out, their hands doing the work. Then let your own unpaid work come to mind too, the things nobody counts, and hold both without a ledger. If you pray, you can hold that person in your tradition's words.
Unpaid. Work done without wages, caring, housework, volunteering, that is still real work, and honored in the old texts and traditions. Today's word.
Your line: I saw what you did, and it mattered. Work without wages is still work. Day nine hundred twelve.

913.title: Not my worth
913.carry: what was lost was held, not who you are
913.howItsDone: People facing job loss often lean on community, faith or philosophy to keep their sense of worth apart from their work; Stoic readers return to Epictetus's sorting of what is and isn't in our power, and Jewish and Christian readers turn to the book of Job.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was unpaid: work nobody pays for, from dishes to langar. Your line was I saw what you did, and it mattered. Today, what's left of a person when the work is gone.
screen: `I SAW WHAT YOU DID, AND IT MATTERED.`

segments.voice: The badge stops working at the door. Or the shop that was going to last forever puts a sign in the window. Or the body says no more to the job it did for years. However it comes, losing work can feel like losing a name. Someone asks what you do, and for a while there's no easy answer. Today: Epictetus.
screen: `THE BADGE STOPS WORKING.` → `SO WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `NO EASY ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, the confusion. A job gives us a schedule, colleagues, a title, a paycheck and a ready answer at parties. It's easy to fuse all of that into a sense of who we are. When the job goes, it can seem as if we've gone with it. Second, a Stoic teacher. Epictetus taught philosophy in the Roman world. His handbook opens with a sorting: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Not in our power: our body, our property, our reputation, our offices, the positions we hold. In our power: how we judge, what we aim for, what we turn away from. For Epictetus, a person's worth lives on that inside list. A job is on the outside list: given and taken, never the measure of a person. Third, a man who lost everything. In the book of Job, in the Hebrew Bible, Job loses his wealth, his household, his children, all in one day. And he says, "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Later in the book he argues, mourns and protests at length, and the text lets him. Some readers hear a distinction in that first line: what was given can be taken, and the one it was given to is still there. Fourth, what this is not. It isn't a claim that losing work doesn't hurt. Rent and purpose matter. Grief is fair, and Job is given room for it. Epictetus would ask for a cooler sorting. What the two share is a narrower line: what was lost was held, not who you are, and the person who held it is still there.
screen: `A JOB FUSED WITH A SELF.` · `IN OUR POWER, AND NOT.` · `THE LORD GAVE, AND HATH TAKEN.` · `IT HURTS, AND IT'S NOT YOUR WORTH.` · then, large: `NOT MY WORTH.`

segments.voice: Picture two baskets, and into the outer one gently set the things that can be given and taken: a title, a desk, a salary, how others see you. Then notice what's left in you: how you pay attention, what you care about, how you meet this day. That's the inner basket; rest there.
Epictetus. The Stoic teacher who sorted the world into what's in our power and what isn't, and put a job on the outside list. Today's word.
Your line: what was lost was held, not who you are. It hurts; it isn't your worth. See you tomorrow.

914.title: The stopping days
914.hook: Friday prayers, Shabbat, Sunday, Buddhist observance days: many traditions stop work on purpose
914.howItsDone: Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall; Muslims gather for the Friday congregational prayer at midday; Christians commonly gather on Sunday, and some keep it as a day of rest; Buddhist lay followers may keep extra precepts on uposatha days.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Epictetus, with his two lists, and a job on the outside one. Your line was what was lost was held, not who you are. Today, the days when work stops on purpose.
screen: `WHAT WAS LOST WAS HELD, NOT WHO YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: A Friday at midday, and a shopkeeper pulls down the shutter and walks toward the mosque. A Friday at sunset, and a family lights candles and the phones go into a drawer. A Sunday morning, and church bells over quiet streets. A full-moon day, and a woman in white walks to a Buddhist temple to keep extra precepts until the next morning. Different calendars, different reasons. But each is a stopping, chosen on purpose and kept together. Today: uposatha.
screen: `A SHUTTER, CANDLES, BELLS, WHITE.` → `DIFFERENT CALENDARS.` → `STOPPING ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Each tradition stops in its own way. First, Shabbat. The Ten Commandments in Exodus say, "Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work." Then the verse keeps going: not you, nor your son or daughter, nor your servants, nor your animals, nor the stranger within your gates. The rest is for everyone in the household, including those who work for you. Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. Second, Friday in Islam. The Qur'an tells believers, when the call to the Friday congregational prayer is heard, to hurry to the remembrance of God and leave their trading; and when the prayer is done, to go out and seek God's bounty again. So Friday isn't a full day off; it's a stopping in the middle of the day, for prayer together. Third, Sunday. The book of Revelation speaks of being "in the Spirit on the Lord's day," and Christian tradition came to read the Lord's day as Sunday, the day of the resurrection. Some Christians keep it as a day of rest; others gather and then go about the day; and some, such as Seventh-day Adventists, keep the seventh day, Saturday. Fourth, Buddhist observance days, called uposatha. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha teaches lay followers to keep extra precepts on these days, for a night and a day, following the example of the awakened ones. These days don't ask for the same thing. What they share is a refusal to let work fill every hour.
screen: `SHABBAT: REST FOR EVERYONE.` · `FRIDAY: LEAVE YOUR TRADING.` · `SUNDAY: THE LORD'S DAY.` · `UPOSATHA: EXTRA PRECEPTS.` · then, large: `THE STOPPING DAYS.`

segments.voice: Let your hands fall still, and if something in you is still working, planning, answering, let it hear the shutter come down. Then gently look ahead at your week for an afternoon, an evening or a morning that could become a stopping time, kept on purpose. Don't schedule it yet; just find it, and imagine the quiet in it.
uposatha. A Buddhist observance day kept with extra precepts, one of the ways traditions set apart time from work on purpose. Today's word.
Your line: chosen on purpose, kept together. Different calendars, different reasons. Day nine hundred fourteen, done.

915.title: Wealth used well
915.hook: the Buddha praises wealth earned rightly and shared (Anguttara Nikaya 4.61); Paul warns of loving money (1 Timothy 6:10)
915.howItsDone: Buddhist householders read the Buddha's teaching on right use of wealth as a guide to providing for family and giving; some Christians turn to 1 Timothy 6 when thinking about money, generosity and contentment.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was uposatha, a Buddhist observance day, one of the ways work stops on purpose. Your line was chosen on purpose, kept together. Today, what work leaves in our hands: money.

"Money is the root of all evil." The line gets passed around as if it were scripture. It isn't, quite. The real verse says something sharper. And from a very different tradition comes a teaching that sounds almost the opposite at first: the Buddha speaking warmly to a householder about earning and enjoying wealth. Put the two side by side, and they turn out to ask a similar question. Not whether you have money. What it's doing. Today: Anathapindika.
screen: `THE ROOT OF ALL EVIL?` → `NOT QUITE.` → `WHAT IS IT DOING?`

segments.voice: First, the verse as it actually reads. In the first letter to Timothy, which tradition ascribes to Paul: "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows." The love of money, not money itself. The problem is where the heart is fastened. Second, the same letter, a few lines later. Those who are rich are told not to trust in uncertain riches, and to be "rich in good works, ready to distribute." The letter doesn't tell the rich to stop being rich. It tells them what wealth is for. Third, the Buddha to a householder. In a discourse in the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha speaks with Anathapindika, a wealthy lay follower. He praises wealth gained by effort and the sweat of the brow, gained rightly, without harm. And he describes what to do with it: make yourself happy, and your parents, your family, the people who work for you and your friends; guard against misfortune like fire and flood; make offerings to relatives, guests and those who have died; and give to those living a holy life. Wealth spent like that, he says, has been put to good use. Fourth, the shared question. The letter to Timothy warns about loving money; the Buddha praises using it well. Neither treats money as holy or as filth. Each points past the money to the person holding it: how it was earned, and where it goes.
screen: `THE LOVE OF MONEY.` · `RICH IN GOOD WORKS.` · `EARNED RIGHTLY, USED WELL.` · `WHAT IS IT DOING?` · then, large: `WEALTH USED WELL.`

segments.voice: Follow your money in a calm, unhurried way: picture where it came from, the work and hours it stands for, and honor that. Then picture where it went this week, without judging any of it. Let one sum come to mind, small or large, that you could spend in a way the Buddha's list would recognize, making someone glad, guarding against hard times or giving, and hold it there.
Anathapindika. The wealthy follower the Buddha taught to earn rightly and spend it on family, guests and those living a holy life. Today's word.
Your line: put to good use. Not whether you have money, but what it's doing. That's day nine hundred fifteen.

916.title: A tenth
916.hook: Christian tithes, Muslim zakat, Sikh dasvandh: each tradition sets aside a share
916.howItsDone: Some Christians tithe a tenth of their income to their church; Muslims calculate and pay zakat each year on qualifying wealth; Sikhs who keep dasvandh set aside a tenth of their earnings, often through the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Anathapindika, the householder the Buddha told to put his wealth to good use. Your line was put to good use. Today, the share some traditions set aside before anything else.

A paycheck lands. Before the rent, before the groceries, a small piece is moved somewhere else: an envelope in a church, a transfer to a mosque's fund for the poor, a donation box at a gurdwara. For some who give this way, it isn't charity left over at the end of the month, if there's anything left. It's set aside on purpose, sometimes before anything else is paid. Today: a tenth.
screen: `A PAYCHECK LANDS.` → `OFF THE TOP.` → `THE FIRST THING PAID.`

segments.voice: First, the tithe. In Genesis, after a battle, Abram meets Melchizedek, a priest and king, and "he gave him tithes of all." The letter to the Hebrews, looking back on that scene, spells it out: Abraham "gave the tenth of the spoils." Later, the prophet Malachi says, "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house." Some Christians today give a tenth of their income to their church; others see the tenth as a guide rather than a rule, and give in their own measure. Second, zakat. The Qur'an pairs prayer with zakat, a required giving, and it names who should receive it, among them the poor, the needy, those in debt and the traveler. Zakat isn't a tenth of income; Muslim teaching sets it as a share of certain kinds of wealth, and the share differs from one kind to another. But like the tithe, it isn't optional generosity. It's an act of worship, and in Muslim teaching it purifies the wealth that remains. Third, dasvandh. In Sikh tradition, dasvandh is the practice of setting aside a tenth of one's earnings for the community and those in need, often given through the gurdwara, where it can help keep the free kitchen running. Fourth, what they share. The amounts and rules differ, and each tradition has its own reasons. But each sets a share aside on purpose and regularly, which turns giving from a mood into a habit. And each, in its own way, treats part of what comes in as belonging to others.

917.title: Ambition, examined
917.howItsDone: Christians read Mark 10:43–44 as a teaching that greatness means serving others, and Hindus who study the Bhagavad Gita read 2.47 as guidance on working fully without clinging to the results.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was a tenth: the tithe, zakat and dasvandh, each setting a share aside on purpose. Your line was a share for others.

Two brothers walk up to their teacher on the road and ask for a favor before they'll say what it is. In Mark's Gospel they are James and John, fishermen who once left their nets to follow Jesus. The request is blunt: when you come into your glory, let one of us sit at your right hand, and the other at your left. The other ten hear about it, and Mark says they are much displeased. Mark doesn't say why. Some readers suspect the ten wanted the same seats. Today: ambition.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS ASK A FAVOR.` → `THE RIGHT HAND AND THE LEFT.` → `THE TEN ARE DISPLEASED.`

segments.voice: First, what Jesus doesn't do. He doesn't tell them to stop wanting to be great. He calls them to him and turns the ladder upside down. In the King James Bible: "whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: and whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all." Ambition isn't erased. It's handed a job. Second, a voice that climbed all the way up. Ecclesiastes speaks as a king in Jerusalem who built houses, planted vineyards, and gathered silver and gold. Then he looks at all of it: "all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun." He reached what he aimed at, and it couldn't tell him what it was for. Third, a teaching from India. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that his right is to the work itself, never to its fruits; the fruits shouldn't be his motive, and he shouldn't cling to doing nothing either. Some readers hear a way to strive with everything while loosening the grip on the prize. Fourth, the question all three leave on the table. Ambition can serve, or it can consume, and the difference may lie less in how much someone wants than in what the wanting is for. A promotion that lets someone protect a team is one thing; the same promotion as a scoreboard is another. This week asked about shaping a job, unpaid work, worth without work, stopping, money and sharing. Ambition asks the question under all of them.
screen: `THE GREAT ONE SERVES.` · `NO PROFIT UNDER THE SUN.` · `THE WORK, NOT THE FRUITS.` · `SERVE OR CONSUME?` · then, large: `WHAT IS IT FOR?`

segments.voice: Bring one ambition to mind, large or small: a job, a number, a finished project, a name on a door. Ask it plainly, what are you for, and ask the same of each answer until the answers stop changing; safety, love, someone you provide for, wanting to be seen: any of these can be honest. If you pray, hold that last answer in your own tradition's words.
Ambition. The wish to rise. In Mark's Gospel Jesus doesn't forbid it; he points it toward serving. Today's word.
Your line: what is it for. The wish can stay; it just needs a job. Day nine hundred seventeen, done.
